title: Portfolio governance registry
description: Which repositories are governed, and what enforcement configuration each is claimed to have. This file records the ENFORCEMENT CONTRACT, never applicability: whether a standard applies to a repository is decided by that repository's own manifest and the detectors, with evidence reported either way. Every field here must be something the audit can actually check against evidence — a field that cannot be verified would be a claim the audit appears to have confirmed and has not.

repositories.description: Currently governed repositories, keyed by a stable short name. The key is the governance identity and is what the history is compared against; the canonical remote identity lives in 'repository' and may change under it.

repository.description: The canonical remote identity, as owner/name. Compared against the API's own full_name, so a rename is detected rather than followed silently.

rationale.description: Why this repository is governed. Read by a human deciding whether a proposed retirement is reasonable.

workflow.description: Path within the governed repository at which the caller workflow must exist.

reusableWorkflow.description: The reusable workflow path the caller must invoke. Defaults to this repository's validate.yml.

checkName.description: The status check identity the caller produces, as GitHub composes it for a reusable workflow: the calling job's name, then ' / ', then the called job's name. Compared BOTH against what the caller would actually produce and against what the branch actually requires, because those are two different ways for enforcement to break.

protectedBranches.description: Branches whose merges this enforcement is claimed to govern. Each is checked for governance under classic protection and under rulesets independently; the two mechanisms are not equivalent and neither is inferred from the other.

requiredChecks.description: Check identities that must actually be registered as required on every listed branch. A name here that the platform does not require is a stale claim, and a stale claim is an audit failure even when the workflow file itself is perfect.

retired.description: Repositories that were governed and no longer are. Removing a repository from governance is itself a governance change; this is where it is recorded, so that absence never has to be read as a decision nobody wrote down. This records a removal, it does not authorise one — validating authorisation needs an authority outside these repositories, and inventing one here would produce a rubber stamp that looked like governance. Null means none have been retired, which is not the same as the key being absent by oversight.

removedAt.description: The date governance ended, as YYYY-MM-DD.

rationale.description: Why it is no longer governed. A retirement with no reason is a deletion with a label on it, so this may not be empty.
